title: Cutler
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 14 of 40
content:
Danse did not sleep after Fort Strong.

I knew because I did not sleep either.

The Prydwen’s night cycle dimmed the lights but never silenced the ship. Engines thrummed through the deck. Pipes clicked. Boots passed in corridors. The Brotherhood could imitate darkness; it could not imitate rest.

I found Danse in the maintenance bay at 0300 cleaning a weapon that was already clean.

“You missed a spot,” I said.

He did not look up.

“No, I didn’t.”

“I know.”

I sat on the bench opposite him.

He continued running cloth through the rifle barrel.

“You don’t have to stay.”

“Neither do you.”

“I’m working.”

“You’re polishing your emotions.”

His hands stopped.

“That doesn’t make sense.”

“It made sense in my head.”

“That’s concerning.”

I smiled.

He did not, but the tension eased.

For several minutes I watched him work.

Finally he set the rifle down.

“You want to know about Cutler.”

“I want you to tell me whatever keeps you from dismantling that gun into atoms.”

Danse leaned back.

“The first time I met him, he tried to sell me my own scrap.”

I blinked.

“What?”

“In Rivet City. I had a box of servo parts beside my stand. Walked away for maybe two minutes. When I came back, Cutler was trying to sell them to a customer.”

“That’s incredible.”

“I nearly broke his nose.”

“Also incredible.”

“He said if I left valuable inventory unattended, I deserved to lose it.”

“What happened?”

“I made him give me half the caps.”

I laughed.

Danse smiled down at his hands.

“We became partners three days later.”

The story came slowly after that.

Rivet City markets. Junk runs through dangerous buildings. Splitting food when one of them had a bad week. Competing over who could find the strangest pre-War object and convincing tourists it had value.

“Cutler once sold a broken hand dryer as a ‘portable wind generator.’”

“Did it work?”

“No.”

“Did the customer know?”

“Eventually.”

“Your Brotherhood origin story involves fraud.”

“Minor misrepresentation.”

I laughed so hard someone in the next bay told us to shut up.

Danse looked younger when he spoke about those years.

Then the story reached recruitment.

“The Brotherhood came through Rivet City looking for people who could handle themselves. Cutler heard ‘regular meals’ and decided immediately.”

“And you?”

“I heard ‘training.’”

“Of course you did.”

“We thought we had nothing to lose.”

His smile faded.

“That’s usually when people discover how much they had.”

The maintenance bay seemed colder.

Danse stared at the rifle on the table.

“Years later, when I found him in that nest, he looked at me.”

I did not move.

“His face was changing. His voice…” Danse swallowed. “I don’t know if he knew me.”

“You said he didn’t attack.”

“He didn’t.”

“Did he speak?”

“Not clearly.”

Danse rubbed both hands over his face.

“I fired before he finished changing.”

The sentence came out broken around the edges.

I moved to the bench beside him.

Not touching.

Close.

“I told myself it was mercy.”

“Maybe it was.”

“I told myself there was no person left to save.”

“Maybe there wasn’t.”

He looked at me, frustrated.

“You keep saying maybe.”

“Because certainty would be a lie.”

His anger collapsed.

“Yes.”

He looked down.

“That’s what I hate.”

“The not knowing?”

“The possibility that I could be wrong and still have done something irreversible.”

There it was.

Not hatred of mutants.

Fear of being the person who obeyed the rule and killed his friend anyway.

I reached for his hand.

This time I did it slowly enough that he could move away.

He did not.

My fingers closed around his.

Danse stared at them.

“I don’t know what Cutler was in those last minutes,” I said. “But I know what he was before. Your friend. The person who knew you before the armor. Remembering that doesn’t betray the Brotherhood.”

His thumb shifted against mine.

“No.”

“And questioning what happened doesn’t either.”

“That part is debatable.”

“Then debate me.”

His mouth twisted.

“At three in the morning?”

“Coward.”

He gave me a tired, real smile.

Our hands were still joined.

Neither of us acknowledged it.

Eventually Danse said, “He would have made fun of me.”

“For what?”

“This.”

He lifted our hands slightly.

My heart tripped.

“Why?”

“Because I’m terrible at this.”

“At holding hands?”

“At…”

He gestured vaguely between us with his free hand.

“This.”

I decided mercy was appropriate.

“Talking?”

“Yes.”

“Terrible.”

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.”

I started to pull away.

His fingers tightened.

Just for a second.

Then he released me.

The absence of contact felt louder than it should have.

Danse picked up the rifle again.

He did not resume cleaning it.

“I haven’t told anyone that much about him.”

“I know.”

“How?”

“Because you looked like it hurt.”

He stared at me.

Then nodded once.

“Get some sleep.”

“That sounds like an order.”

“It is.”

“You coming?”

The words left my mouth before I considered them.

Danse’s eyes widened.

I felt heat climb my face.

“To the sleeping quarters,” I added quickly. “To sleep. Separately.”

“Yes.” His voice cracked slightly. He cleared his throat. “Obviously.”

We walked back together without speaking.

At my bunk, he paused.

“Good night.”

“Good night, Danse.”

He started away.

I lay down beneath the pipes.

Ten seconds later, from the corridor, I heard him mutter, “Outstanding.”

I buried my face in the blanket so no one would hear me laugh.

The next morning I found him in the Prydwen’s mess with coffee so black it looked structurally unsound.

He had told me about Cutler during the night: Rivet City, the Brotherhood, the patrol, the super mutants, the thing he had been forced to do when the man he loved like a brother was no longer entirely the man he remembered.

Now Danse stared into the cup like the answer might be at the bottom.

I sat across from him.

“Did you sleep?”

“Yes.”

“Liar.”

“Approximately forty minutes.”

“That is not sleep. That is losing an argument with consciousness.”

He made a sound that might have been amusement.

I took the coffee from his hand and tasted it.

My entire mouth objected.

“What is wrong with you?”

Danse looked genuinely confused.

“It’s coffee.”

“It’s a chemical weapon.”

“It’s efficient.”

“Food should not be evaluated by tactical efficiency.”

“Coffee is not food.”

“That is the first sensible thing you’ve said about it.”

He took the cup back.

The absurdity helped.

For a while.

Then he said, “I should have found them sooner.”

There it was.

“You told me the patrol disappeared in an irradiated area full of super mutants.”

“I should have anticipated the route.”

“You weren’t even commanding the mission.”

“I was his friend.”

The sentence cracked in the middle.

Danse looked away quickly.

I did not tell him it was not his fault.

He would have rejected that because grief is not a courtroom and guilt does not care about evidence.

Instead I asked, “What would Cutler say if he heard you taking responsibility for the Commonwealth existing around him?”

Danse’s mouth tightened.

“He’d tell me to stop being an idiot.”

“Sounds wise.”

“He was not.”

The smile came anyway.

“What was he like before?”

Danse leaned back.

“Reckless.”

“Compared to you, a chair is reckless.”

“He cheated at target competitions.”

“How?”

“He’d adjust the sights on my rifle when I wasn’t looking.”

I laughed.

Danse did too.

Then his eyes turned wet.

He looked furious about it.

“I remember the last time I saw him as himself more clearly than I remember some entire years of my life.”

I reached across the table.

My hand stopped halfway.

Choice.

Danse looked at it.

Then placed his hand in mine.

His grip was careful at first.

Then not.

“I’m afraid,” he said quietly, “that if I let myself care about people the way I cared about him, I’ll lose them the same way.”

“That’s possible.”

He looked down at our hands as if he had only just realized he was still holding mine.

“Cutler used to say I could turn anything into an assignment,” he said.

“Was he wrong?”

“No.” A faint smile. “He once ordered me to take an afternoon off.”

“That is deeply funny.”

“I told him he lacked authority.”

“What did he do?”

“Stole my boots.”

I laughed so suddenly a nearby knight glanced over.

Danse’s smile widened before grief pulled at it.

“I found them hanging from a pipe in Rivet City.”

The memory hurt him.

It also warmed him.

For once I did not try to separate those things.

He flinched at the answer.

I held on.

“I’m not going to promise the Commonwealth can’t take people. It can. You know that better than I do.”

“Then why—”

“Because not caring doesn’t save them.”

His gaze dropped to our joined hands.

“It only makes you lose them early.”

Danse went very still.

Around us, soldiers ate breakfast, complained about duty shifts, and argued about ammunition requisitions. Life continued with rude efficiency.

Finally his thumb moved across my knuckles.

“You have an irritating habit of making arguments I can’t easily dismiss.”

“You could try bad coffee.”

“That is not an argument.”

“Neither is this beverage.”

The laugh that came out of him was quiet and tired and real.

He did not release my hand until his coffee had gone cold.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
